d: Investing in companies built on scientific or engineering breakthroughs (semiconductors, quantum, advanced materials, biotech, space, energy). Longer development, higher capital needs and technical risk, with defensibility from IP and know-how.
x: A fusion energy startup raising $100m before revenue.
A quantum sensing spin-out from a university lab.
s: A deep-tech company needs seven years to reach revenue.
Fund term, reserves and syndicate depth must fit the long path; generalist VC timelines often do not.
Value depends on the next proof point; staged financing limits losses.

d: A 1–9 scale, originally from NASA and used by the EU, describing how mature a technology is, from basic principles (1) to proven in operation (9). Deep-tech investors use it to stage risk and capital.
x: A battery chemistry at TRL 4 (lab validation).
A satellite subsystem at TRL 7 (demonstrated in space).
s: Startup at TRL 3 asks for a large Series A.
Investors may prefer grants or a smaller seed until TRL 5–6.
EU funding calls often target specific TRL ranges.

d: Checking that a company owns or can use the intellectual property it depends on: patent ownership and scope, licences from universities, freedom to operate, and inventor assignments.
x: Confirming a university licence is exclusive and worldwide.
A freedom-to-operate opinion before a medtech investment.
s: Founders' patents are owned by their former employer.
The deal stalls until ownership is fixed.
A competitor's patent blocks the product.
Freedom-to-operate risk cuts the valuation or kills the deal.

d: A company formed to commercialise research from a university, usually with a licence or assignment of IP from the university's technology transfer office, which often takes equity.
x: A spin-out with the university holding 10% equity.
A licence with royalties of 2% of sales.
s: High stakes can deter investors; negotiation follows market norms.
Founding professor stays at the university.
Time commitment and conflict rules matter.

d: Money that does not cost equity, such as research grants, innovation loans and tax credits. Important for deep-tech companies to reach milestones before raising equity.
x: An EIC Accelerator grant plus equity component.
R&D tax credits refunded in cash.
s: Equity needs fall, improving founder and investor ownership.

d: An organisation that creates startups internally, providing ideas, team and early capital, then spins them out with outside investors. The studio keeps a large founding stake.
x: A studio launching four companies a year.
Studio taking 30% founder equity.
s: High studio stakes can leave founders under-incentivised.
Fund invests in a studio's companies.

d: A fixed-term programme that invests small amounts in cohorts of startups for equity, with mentoring and a demo day.
x: $500k for a set percentage via SAFE.
A corporate accelerator in energy.

d: Minority or control investments in profitable or near-profitable fast-growing companies, with little or no leverage. Sits between late-stage venture and buyout.
x: A €50m minority stake in a profitable SaaS company.
A growth round funding international expansion.
s: Protective provisions and exit rights matter.

d: Holding less than control, relying on contractual rights (board seats, vetoes, exit rights) rather than majority voting.
x: A 25% stake with two board seats.
A minority stake in a family business.
s: Exit depends on drag, put or IPO rights.
Minority investor can only veto reserved matters.

d: Owning a majority or otherwise controlling the company, allowing the fund to set strategy, change management and decide exit timing. Typical of buyouts.
x: A 70% buyout stake.
Control via board majority.
s: Control lets the fund replace them.

d: Buying a division from a larger company and setting it up as a standalone business, often with transitional services from the seller.
x: A PE fund buying a chemicals division.
Transitional services agreement for IT and payroll.
s: Returns fall; carve-out complexity was underpriced.

d: A fund acquires a listed company and delists it, following takeover rules on offer price, disclosure and minority squeeze-out.
x: A UK P2P under the Takeover Code.
Delisting an Indian company under SEBI delisting rules.
s: Bid fails or price is raised.

d: Showing which deals each team member led and what part of a prior firm's results they can fairly claim. LPs verify attribution through references and documents.
x: A partner claiming 6 of 15 deals from a prior fund.
An attribution letter from the former employer.
s: Former employer refuses to confirm attribution.
LPs rely on board records and references.
Two partners claim the same deal.
LPs see inconsistency as a red flag.

d: An internal body, functionally independent of the deal team, that reviews and approves quarterly valuations under the valuation policy.
x: CFO, risk officer and an independent member reviewing marks.
Quarterly committee minutes.
s: Deal partner pushes a high mark.

d: LPA limits on what the fund may invest in: sectors, geographies, instruments, listed securities, hostile deals, and maximums per company.
x: No more than 20% outside Europe.
No investments in tobacco or weapons.
s: Attractive deal in an excluded sector.

d: The duty of loyalty and care a manager owes. In US law advisers owe fiduciary duties to their clients (the funds); LPAs may modify duties to the extent law allows.
x: SEC position that advisers cannot waive fiduciary duty entirely.
Delaware LPAs narrowing GP duties.
s: GP favours its own interests in a CV.

d: Policies and diligence to prevent bribery by the manager or portfolio companies, under laws such as the US FCPA, UK Bribery Act, France's Sapin II and India's Prevention of Corruption Act.
x: ABC diligence on a company selling to governments.
Training for portfolio management.
s: Target pays agents for government contracts.
Deeper diligence; deal may be dropped.

d: Investing with the intention to generate measurable social or environmental impact alongside financial return. Often uses impact management frameworks such as the Operating Principles for Impact Management.
x: An energy access fund in Africa.
Impact-linked carry tied to targets.
s: GP earns full carry only if targets are met.

d: Whether an investment causes an outcome that would not have happened otherwise. A test for impact claims.
x: Financing a project banks would not fund.
Providing first-loss capital.
s: Fund buys a listed green stock.

d: An industry initiative of GPs and LPs to standardise portfolio-company ESG metrics (emissions, diversity, work-related injuries and others) for private markets.
x: Collecting Scope 1 and 2 emissions from portfolio companies.
Reporting board diversity metrics.
s: LPs ask for comparable ESG data.
EDCI metrics give a common format.
GP estimates and improves over time.

d: SFDR indicators of negative sustainability effects of investments, such as greenhouse gas emissions or board gender diversity, disclosed at entity or product level.
x: PAI statement for a large AIFM.
Product-level PAI consideration for an Article 8 fund.
s: Entity-level PAI may be optional, with explanation.
Proposal reinstates product-level PAIs for some categories.

d: The EU classification of environmentally sustainable economic activities, with technical criteria. Funds disclose what share of investments is taxonomy-aligned.
x: A renewables fund reporting 80% taxonomy alignment.
Article 9 fund disclosing alignment.

d: An organisation managing a wealthy family's investments. Family offices are flexible, can move fast and often back emerging managers and co-investments, but have smaller teams.
x: A Monaco single-family office investing €20m a year in funds.
An Indian multi-family office anchoring an AIF.
s: Family office wants board seats in companies.
Co-investment or direct deals suit it better than a blind pool.
Commitments to new funds may stop suddenly.

d: A state-owned investment fund, often among the largest LPs, with long horizons and appetite for large co-investments and SMAs.
x: A Gulf SWF committing $500m to a buyout fund.
An SWF taking a GP stake.
s: Manager weighs customisation against the flagship.

d: Retirement schemes investing for members. Large, long-term LPs that care about fees, governance and reporting, often advised by consultants.
x: A Dutch pension with a 15% private markets target.
A US state pension's PE programme.
s: Public pension subject to disclosure laws.

d: An approach, associated with Yale, allocating heavily to private markets and alternatives for long-term institutions, relying on illiquidity premium and manager selection.
x: A university endowment with 40% in private equity and VC.
Foundation adopting similar allocations.
s: Endowments faced capital calls and fell short of cash.
Access to top managers is harder.

d: Insurers invest in private markets under capital rules such as Solvency II in the EU, which set capital charges by asset type. They favour credit and infrastructure.
x: An insurer investing in private credit for yield.
Rated feeder notes to reduce capital charges.
s: Insurer prefers credit or rated structures.

d: Government-backed institutions investing in emerging markets for development and returns, such as IFC, British International Investment and Proparco. They anchor funds and impose ESG standards.
x: IFC anchoring an Indian growth fund.
DFI requiring IFC Performance Standards.
s: Fund adopts environmental and social management system.

d: A US closed-end investment company that lends to or invests in middle-market companies, often listed or non-traded, with pass-through tax treatment.
x: A listed BDC lending to mid-market firms.
A non-traded BDC for wealth clients.

d: A securitisation of leveraged loans into rated tranches, from AAA to equity. A major buyer of buyout debt.
x: A €400m CLO with AAA to equity tranches.
CLO equity fund.
s: Managers retain a share under EU rules.

d: Funding repaid as a percentage of revenue until a cap is reached, used by recurring-revenue businesses as an alternative to equity.
x: Repay 1.5x via 6% of monthly revenue.
RBF for an e-commerce company.

d: A long-term contract to buy electricity from a generator at an agreed price, giving renewable projects predictable revenue that supports financing.
x: A 15-year corporate PPA for a solar farm.
A government auction PPA in India.

d: Exposure to market prices when an asset sells output without a fixed-price contract. Higher return potential and volatility.
x: A wind farm selling 40% of output at spot prices.
Merchant tail after PPA expiry.

d: Financing vessels through bank loans, leasing, export credit, bonds or private funds. Values follow charter rates and are cyclical; assets are mobile and registered under flags.
x: A fund buying dry bulk vessels with 50% debt.
Chinese leasing companies financing tankers.
s: Vessel values and loan covenants are hit.
Older vessels lose value; retrofits or new builds needed.

d: An owner sells an asset (property, vessel, equipment) and leases it back, releasing capital while keeping use. Investors receive lease income.
x: Shipping company selling vessels to a lessor on 10-year bareboat charters.
Retailer selling stores to a real estate fund.
s: Investor repossesses and re-lets the asset.

d: A hedge fund strategy buying stocks expected to rise and shorting those expected to fall, aiming for returns less tied to the market.
x: 130% long, 70% short.
Sector-focused long/short fund.
s: Shorts lose; net exposure determines result.

d: A US registered closed-end fund that offers to repurchase a set share of shares at intervals (often 5% quarterly), used to give wealth investors access to private assets.
x: An interval fund holding private credit.
A tender-offer fund of PE secondaries.

d: An entrepreneur raises capital from investors to search for, buy and run one small company. Investors fund the search, then get the right to invest in the acquisition.
x: Searcher raises $500k for a two-year search.
Acquiring a $10m revenue business.

d: Annual cash distributions as a percentage of NAV or invested capital, important for credit, infrastructure and real estate funds.
x: 8% annual cash yield from a credit fund.
5% yield from core infrastructure.

d: In deal-by-deal waterfalls, realised losses and write-downs on earlier deals are recovered before carry is paid on later winners.
x: Carry on a €20m gain reduced by a prior €8m loss.
Write-downs counted as losses for carry tests.
s: Without carryforward, GP takes carry on the winner regardless.
LPAs differ on whether they count.
